items.title: Missing approver signature delayed programme by 4 weeks
items.description: An AIP submission for a highway bridge was returned because the Technical Approval Authority (TAA) signature was missing. The document had been through full design and Category III check but nobody noticed the approver block was empty. Resubmission took 4 weeks due to the TAA's review backlog.
items.recommendation: Always verify the approver field is completed with name, signature, and date before submission. Add a pre-submission checklist that specifically checks all signature blocks.

items.title: Wrong Eurocode National Annex caused redesign
items.description: A structural design used the default Eurocode parameters instead of the UK National Annex values. The concrete cover was 10mm less than required under UK NA, affecting durability. Full redesign of reinforcement was required.
items.recommendation: Always verify that UK National Annex (NA) values are used, not the default Eurocode recommended values. Check NA to BS EN 1992-1-1 Table NA.1.

items.title: Groundwater level underestimated causing basement flooding during construction
items.description: A basement design used a groundwater level from a desk study rather than actual borehole data. During excavation, groundwater was 2.3m higher than assumed. Emergency dewatering cost £450K and delayed the programme by 8 weeks.
items.recommendation: Always verify groundwater levels against actual GI borehole data, not desk study assumptions. Require seasonal groundwater monitoring for deep excavations.

items.title: Superseded standard referenced in design — caught at Category III check
items.description: A design report referenced BS 8110 for concrete design instead of BS EN 1992 (Eurocode 2). BS 8110 was withdrawn in 2010. The Category III checker caught it, but the redesign to Eurocode 2 took 3 weeks.
items.recommendation: Maintain a current standards register. Check all referenced standards against BSI and verify they have not been withdrawn or superseded.

items.title: No temporary works design caused retaining wall failure
items.description: A secant pile retaining wall was designed for the permanent condition but no temporary propping design was provided. During excavation, the wall deflected 85mm (limit was 25mm), cracking adjacent utilities. Emergency propping was installed at £280K cost.
items.recommendation: Every design for retaining structures must include a temporary works assessment. Construction stages must be explicitly modelled — the temporary condition is often more critical than permanent.
